title: Energy Follows Thought: The Stories Behind My Songs
author: Willie Nelson
critics_take: Willie Nelson gathers the lyrics of more than 150 of his songs, each paired with a short account of when and why he wrote it, written with David Ritz and Mickey Raphael. Reviewers treated it as an affectionate companion to his catalog and memoirs, valued more for its anecdotes and lyrics on the page than as a sustained narrative.

title: Rites of Passage
author: William Golding
critics_take: The first volume of Golding's sea trilogy (later collected as To the Ends of the Earth), told through the journal of a young gentleman, Edmund Talbot, on a voyage to Australia in the early 1800s, where a clergyman's humiliation aboard ship becomes a study of class and cruelty. It won the 1980 Booker Prize, and critics praised its period voice and its moral seriousness about shipboard hierarchy.

title: Light in August
author: William Faulkner
critics_take: Faulkner's novel braids the stories of Lena Grove, a pregnant young woman searching for the father of her child, and Joe Christmas, a drifter of uncertain racial identity, in Yoknapatawpha County. Critics regard it as one of his major works and one of his most direct treatments of race, violence and Southern Calvinism, more accessible in form than The Sound and the Fury.

title: Candide
author: Voltaire
critics_take: Voltaire's satirical tale follows the naive Candide through war, earthquake, the Inquisition and shipwreck while his tutor Pangloss insists that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. It is regarded as a classic of the Enlightenment, admired for its speed and wit and for its attack on Leibnizian optimism, ending with the famous advice to cultivate one's garden.

title: Bharata Sindhu Rashmi (ಭಾರತ ಸಿಂಧು ರಶ್ಮಿ)
author: V. K. Gokak
critics_take: Gokak's long epic poem in Kannada, built around the Vedic age and the figure of the sage Vishvamitra, is one of the longest epics written in modern Indian literature. It was cited when Gokak received the Jnanpith Award for 1990; critics respect its ambition and its visionary Aurobindo-influenced outlook, though its length and density have kept its readership small.

title: Samakshama (ಸಮಕ್ಷಮ)
author: U. R. Ananthamurthy
critics_take: A 1980 Kannada prose collection by U. R. Ananthamurthy, from the period when his critical essays were helping to shape the Navya movement. Little published criticism of this particular volume exists in English; it is read mainly alongside his better-known novels and essays.

title: Kaalamaana (ಕಾಲಮಾನ)
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: Valmikiya Nevadalli (ವಾಲ್ಮೀಕಿಯ ನೆವದಲ್ಲಿ)
author: U. R. Ananthamurthy
critics_take: A late Kannada essay collection by U. R. Ananthamurthy that uses Valmiki and the Ramayana tradition as a starting point for reflections on literature, culture and politics. Little published criticism of this volume exists in English; it is generally read as part of his public intellectual work rather than his fiction.

title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
author: Tracy Chevalier
critics_take: A historical novel imagining the story behind Vermeer's painting, told by Griet, a young maid in the painter's household in 1660s Delft. It became an international bestseller and was filmed in 2003; reviewers praised its quiet, painterly prose and sense of period, though some found its drama deliberately muted.

title: Wild Bill: The True Story of the American Frontier's First Gunfighter
author: Tom Clavin
critics_take: A popular biography of James Butler "Wild Bill" Hickok, from Civil War scout and lawman to his killing in Deadwood in 1876, trying to separate the man from the legend. Reviewers found it brisk and entertaining in the narrative-history style Clavin is known for, though not a work of new scholarship.

title: Against the Day
author: Thomas Pynchon
critics_take: Pynchon's 1,000-plus-page novel ranges from the 1893 Chicago World's Fair to the years after World War I, mixing anarchist dynamite families, balloonists, mathematicians and pastiche of boys' adventure fiction. Critics were sharply divided: some called it a dazzling summation of his themes, while others found it bloated and exhausting.

title: Vineland
author: Thomas Pynchon
critics_take: Pynchon's first novel after Gravity's Rainbow is set in Reagan-era northern California, where ex-hippie Zoyd Wheeler and his daughter Prairie are drawn into the past of her radical-filmmaker mother and a federal prosecutor's vendetta. After a 17-year wait many reviewers found it slight and disappointing, though later critics have defended its comedy and its critique of state power and television culture.

title: ಯುದ್ಧಯಾತ್ರೆ (Yuddhayatre)
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: A Manual of Self Unfoldment
author: Swami Chinmayananda
critics_take: A structured introduction to Vedanta by the founder of the Chinmaya Mission, laying out the nature of the self, the mind and the paths of spiritual practice in a course-like format. It is widely used in Chinmaya Mission study groups; outside that setting there is little independent critical coverage.

title: Kindle Life
author: Swami Chinmayananda
critics_take: A short book of Vedantic guidance by Swami Chinmayananda on living purposefully, covering discipline, the mind and the pursuit of the spiritual goal in everyday terms. It is popular as an entry-level text within the Chinmaya Mission; little independent published criticism exists.

title: "So What Are You Going to Do with That?": Finding Careers Outside Academia
author: Susan Basalla and Maggie Debelius
critics_take: A practical guide for PhDs and graduate students leaving academia, covering how to reframe academic skills, network, write résumés and handle interviews, illustrated with profiles of people who made the move. It has been reissued in updated editions by the University of Chicago Press and is often recommended in graduate career offices as one of the standard books on the subject.

title: Basic Okinawan: From Conversation to Grammar
author: Rumiko Shinzato and Shoichi Iwasaki
critics_take: A textbook of Uchinaaguchi (Okinawan) from the University of Hawai'i Press, built around dialogues with grammar explanations and exercises, for learners who usually already know some Japanese. It has been welcomed as one of the few English-language course books for the endangered language and part of revitalization efforts; formal reviews are still limited.

title: Hit Refresh: The Quest to Rediscover Microsoft's Soul and Imagine a Better Future for Everyone
author: Satya Nadella
critics_take: Microsoft's CEO combines memoir (his upbringing in Hyderabad, his family, his rise at Microsoft) with an account of the company's cultural reset and his views on AI, mixed reality and quantum computing. Reviewers found it sincere and useful on culture change and empathy, but often corporate in tone and cautious about the company's internal conflicts.

title: Dharmashree (ಧರ್ಮಶ್ರೀ)
author: S. L. Bhyrappa
critics_take: One of Bhyrappa's early novels, dealing with religious conversion and the pressures it puts on an individual and a family. It is seen as an early sign of the questions about religion and identity that run through his later work; critical coverage in English is limited.

title: Kavalu (ಕವಲು)
author: S. L. Bhyrappa
critics_take: A Kannada novel about marriage, divorce and family breakdown in urban Karnataka, with a sharp focus on feminism and the law. It was a bestseller and also one of Bhyrappa's most controversial books: admirers praised its frankness, while many critics called it hostile to feminism.

title: Tantu (ತಂತು)
author: S. L. Bhyrappa
critics_take: A long Kannada novel set against the political climate of the Emergency era, following a journalist and the people around him as public and private values erode. Critics count it among Bhyrappa's major social novels, noting its scope and its argument about corruption, though some find it didactic.

title: Daatu (ದಾಟು)
author: S. L. Bhyrappa
critics_take: Bhyrappa's novel about caste in a Karnataka village, centred on a relationship between a Brahmin woman and a man from another caste and the tensions it exposes across generations. It won the Sahitya Akademi Award and is widely regarded as one of his most important works; it has been translated into English as Crossing Over.

title: Muscle: The Gripping Story of Strength and Movement
author: Roy A. Meals
critics_take: An orthopedic hand surgeon's popular-science tour of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle, covering how muscles work, fail, age and respond to training. Reviewers found it lively and pun-filled, a readable follow-up to his earlier book on bones, if sometimes more anecdotal than deep.

title: Mount Rainier National Park
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: A Whack on the Side of the Head: How You Can Be More Creative
author: Roger von Oech
critics_take: A playful, illustrated book on creative thinking that names ten "mental locks" (such as "the right answer" and "that's not logical") and offers exercises to break them. It became a long-running bestseller in business and design circles; readers value it as an accessible primer, while critics note it is light on research.

title: Joseph Conrad: A Biography
author: Roger Tennant
critics_take: A one-volume life of Joseph Conrad, from his Polish childhood and years at sea to his career as an English novelist. It was received as a readable general biography; scholars generally point to the fuller studies by Frederick Karl and Zdzisław Najder as the standard references.

title: Voyage of a Summer Sun: Canoeing the Columbia River
author: Robin Cody
critics_take: Cody's account of paddling the full length of the Columbia River alone, from its source in British Columbia to the Pacific, mixing travel with the river's history, dams and communities. It won an Oregon Book Award and is regarded as a Pacific Northwest classic, praised for its humor and its unsentimental view of a heavily engineered river.

title: I, Claudius
author: Robert Graves
critics_take: A historical novel in the form of the emperor Claudius's own memoir, covering the intrigues of the Julio-Claudian dynasty from Augustus to Caligula. It won the James Tait Black Prize, was adapted into the acclaimed 1976 BBC series, and is widely seen as one of the finest historical novels of the century, though classicists note how heavily it relies on Suetonius and Tacitus's gossip.

title: Collected Stories
author: Roald Dahl
critics_take: The Everyman's Library collection of Dahl's adult short fiction, including the macabre twist-ending stories from Someone Like You, Kiss Kiss and Tales of the Unexpected. Critics admire the stories' cruelty and craftsmanship, and they are often cited as proof that Dahl's adult work is as distinctive as his children's books.

title: Selected Stories
author: Roald Dahl
critics_take: A selection of Dahl's short stories for adults, drawn from the dark, twist-ending tales of Someone Like You and Kiss Kiss. These stories are generally regarded as models of the macabre short story, praised for their economy and black humor.

title: Don't Sweat the Small Stuff... and It's All Small Stuff
author: Richard Carlson
critics_take: A self-help book of 100 short chapters offering simple habits for reducing stress and reacting less to everyday irritations. It was a huge bestseller and spawned a franchise; readers found it calming and practical, while critics called it repetitive and simplistic.

title: Out of My Mind: The Discovery of Saunders-Vixen
author: Richard Bach
critics_take: A short illustrated fable by the author of Jonathan Livingston Seagull about an aviation-minded protagonist and the power of imagination and belief to shape reality. Like Bach's other later books it appealed to readers of his inspirational style but drew little serious critical attention.

title: Alice in Puzzle-Land: A Carrollian Tale for Children Under Eighty
author: Raymond M. Smullyan
critics_take: Smullyan sends Alice, the Tweedles, Humpty Dumpty and other Carroll characters through a series of logic puzzles, from liar-truth-teller riddles to problems about self-reference. Fans of recreational logic count it among his most charming books, written in Carroll's spirit, though the later puzzles are demanding.

title: Arms & Armour of India, Nepal & Sri Lanka: Types, Decoration and Symbolism
author: Ravinder Reddy
critics_take: A large illustrated survey of weapons and armour from the Indian subcontinent, drawing on private collections and covering blade types, firearms, armour, decoration and symbolism. Reviewers praised its photography and breadth as a reference for collectors and historians of arms.

title: Random House Japanese-English English-Japanese Dictionary
author: Seigo Nakao
critics_take: A compact two-way dictionary for English speakers, giving Japanese entries in romanization along with kana and kanji. Learners value it as an affordable, portable dictionary, though reviewers note its limited depth compared with larger references.

title: Bhagawad Geeta: The Gospel of Timeless Wisdom
author: Prabha Duneja
critics_take: An English rendering and commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, verse by verse, aimed at modern readers who want to apply its teachings to everyday life. It is used in devotional and study settings; little independent published criticism exists.

title: The Art of the Cocktail: 100 Classic Cocktail Recipes
author: Philip Collins
critics_take: A small illustrated Chronicle Books collection of classic cocktail recipes with short notes on their history. It was received as an attractive gift book and a handy basic reference rather than an in-depth bartending guide.

title: Kasturi Kosha (ಕಸ್ತೂರಿ ಕೋಶ) - Kannada-Kannada dictionary
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: Stardust
author: Neil Gaiman
critics_take: A fairy tale for adults in which young Tristran Thorn crosses the wall out of the village of Wall into Faerie to bring back a fallen star, who turns out to be a woman named Yvaine. Critics praised it as a witty homage to Victorian fantasy in the line of Lord Dunsany; it was filmed in 2007.

title: Okinawan-English Wordbook: A Short Lexicon of the Okinawan Language with English Definitions and Japanese Cognates
author: Mitsugu Sakihara
critics_take: A lexicon of Shuri Okinawan with English definitions and Japanese cognates, compiled by the historian Mitsugu Sakihara and published by the University of Hawai'i Press. It is regarded as a key English-language reference for learners and researchers of Uchinaaguchi.

title: Tuesdays with Morrie
author: Mitch Albom
critics_take: Sportswriter Mitch Albom's memoir of weekly visits to his old sociology professor Morrie Schwartz, who was dying of ALS, and the lessons on love, work and death they discussed. It became one of the best-selling memoirs ever; readers find it moving, while critics often call it sentimental and simplistic.

title: Farewell Waltz
author: Milan Kundera
critics_take: A darkly comic novel (earlier translated as The Farewell Party) set over five days at a spa town where a trumpeter, a nurse, a doctor running a fertility clinic and a dissident about to emigrate become caught in a farce involving a poison pill. Critics regard it as one of Kundera's most tightly plotted novels, a bleak moral comedy he himself described as a farce.

title: Identity
author: Milan Kundera
critics_take: A short novel, written in French, about a couple, Chantal and Jean-Marc, whose relationship starts to slip after he sends her anonymous love letters. Reviewers found it elegant and thoughtful on identity and perception, but many considered it slight compared with his major works.

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
author: Milan Kundera
critics_take: Kundera's novel follows Tomas, Tereza, Sabina and Franz around the Prague Spring and the Soviet occupation, set against a philosophical meditation on lightness and weight and Nietzsche's eternal return. It is widely considered his masterpiece and a landmark of late-20th-century fiction, admired for its essayistic form, though some critics find its treatment of women and its authorial asides heavy-handed.

title: San Mateo County Coast
author: Michael Smookler
critics_take: A volume in Arcadia Publishing's Images of America series, telling the history of the San Mateo coastside (Montara, Moss Beach, Half Moon Bay and nearby towns) through archival photographs and captions. Like most of the series it is valued as local history; there is little formal criticism.

title: The Stranger in the Woods: The Extraordinary Story of the Last True Hermit
author: Michael Finkel
critics_take: The true story of Christopher Knight, who lived alone in the Maine woods for 27 years, surviving by burglarizing nearby cabins, until his arrest in 2013. Reviewers praised it as a gripping read on solitude, though some questioned the ethics of Finkel's persistent pursuit of a subject who wanted to be left alone.

title: Fearfully and Wonderfully Made: The Astonishing New Science of the Senses
author: Maureen Ann Seaberg
critics_take: A popular-science book on the senses, covering synesthesia, tetrachromacy, supertasters and other people with unusual perception, by a journalist who is herself a synesthete. Reviewers found it engaging and full of surprising cases, though some noted that its enthusiasm sometimes ran ahead of the science.

title: Chikaveera Rajendra (ಚಿಕವೀರ ರಾಜೇಂದ್ರ)
author: Masti Venkatesha Iyengar
critics_take: A historical novel about Chikkavira Rajendra, the last king of Kodagu (Coorg), and his overthrow by the British East India Company in 1834. It was cited for Masti's Jnanpith Award in 1983; critics admire its psychological portrait of a flawed ruler and the moral complexity of its history.

title: Life on the Mississippi
author: Mark Twain
critics_take: Part memoir of Twain's years as an apprentice steamboat pilot before the Civil War and part travelogue of his return to the river two decades later. Critics consider the early piloting chapters some of his finest prose, while the later travel sections are often judged uneven and padded.

title: What They Don't Teach You at Harvard Business School: Notes from a Street-Smart Executive
author: Mark H. McCormack
critics_take: The founder of the sports-management firm IMG offers practical advice on reading people, negotiating, selling and managing, based on his own experience. It was a long-running bestseller; readers praised its common-sense, anecdote-driven style, while critics thought it dated and full of truisms.

title: The Essential Gandhi: An Anthology of His Writings on His Life, Work, and Ideas
author: Mahatma Gandhi; Louis Fischer (ed.)
critics_take: Gandhi's biographer Louis Fischer arranges excerpts from Gandhi's autobiography, letters and articles in roughly chronological order, with linking commentary, to trace his life and thought. It has long been recommended as a reliable one-volume introduction to Gandhi in his own words.

title: Raj: The Making and Unmaking of British India
author: Lawrence James
critics_take: A comprehensive narrative history of British rule in India, from the East India Company's rise to independence and partition in 1947. Reviewers found it detailed and readable, but several critics, especially Indian historians, considered its perspective too sympathetic to the imperial administrators.

title: Kanuru Heggaditi (ಕಾನೂರು ಹೆಗ್ಗಡಿತಿ)
author: Kuvempu
critics_take: Kuvempu's first novel, a broad portrait of a landowning family and village life in the Malnad region, with the forest and the landscape almost as central as the characters. It is regarded as a foundational work of the modern Kannada novel, praised for its scope and depiction of rural society, and was filmed by Girish Karnad in 1999.

title: Hemingway
author: Kenneth S. Lynn
critics_take: A biography of Ernest Hemingway that reads his life and work psychoanalytically, focusing on his relationship with his mother and his anxieties about gender. Critics found it bold and provocative; some praised it as the most insightful Hemingway biography of its time, while others thought it reductive.

title: A Human's Guide to Machine Intelligence: How Algorithms Are Shaping Our Lives and How We Can Stay in Control
author: Kartik Hosanagar
critics_take: A Wharton professor explains how recommendation and decision algorithms work, why they produce unexpected and biased results, and proposes an "algorithmic bill of rights". Reviewers found it a clear, balanced introduction for general readers, though not very technical.

title: Innonde Daari (ಇನ್ನೊಂದೇ ದಾರಿ)
author: K. Shivarama Karanth
critics_take: A Kannada novel by K. Shivarama Karanth, one of his large body of social fiction. Little published criticism of this particular novel exists in English; it is read mainly as part of Karanth's wider work rather than as one of his major titles.

title: Shape: The Hidden Geometry of Information, Biology, Strategy, Democracy, and Everything Else
author: Jordan Ellenberg
critics_take: The mathematician who wrote How Not to Be Wrong shows how geometry, broadly understood, applies to pandemics, gerrymandering, machine learning, games and random walks. Reviewers praised its humor and range, though some found it digressive and less focused than his earlier book.

title: The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness
author: Jonathan Haidt
critics_take: Haidt argues that the shift from play-based to phone-based childhood in the early 2010s drove a sharp rise in teen anxiety and depression, and proposes norms such as no smartphones before high school. It was a major bestseller that influenced policy on school phone bans, but some researchers, notably Candice Odgers in Nature, criticized it for overstating causal evidence.

title: The Exploration of the Colorado River and Its Canyons
author: John Wesley Powell
critics_take: Powell's account of his 1869 expedition down the Green and Colorado rivers through the Grand Canyon, the first known descent, with descriptions of the canyon country's geology. It is regarded as a classic of American exploration writing, though historians note that Powell merged events from his 1869 and 1871-72 trips and played down his crew's role.

title: Bruce Lee: Artist of Life
author: Bruce Lee; John Little (ed.)
critics_take: A volume of the Bruce Lee Library collecting Lee's essays, notes, letters and poems on philosophy, martial arts and self-actualization, edited by John Little. Martial artists value it for showing the reading behind Jeet Kune Do, from Taoism to Krishnamurti; critics note that it is a compilation of fragments rather than a finished work.

title: A Confederacy of Dunces
author: John Kennedy Toole
critics_take: A comic novel about Ignatius J. Reilly, an obese, medievalist misfit living with his mother in New Orleans and stumbling through a series of jobs. Published 11 years after Toole's suicide through the efforts of his mother and Walker Percy, it won the 1981 Pulitzer Prize and is widely regarded as a classic of American comic fiction.

title: The Tao of Leadership: Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching Adapted for a New Age
author: John Heider
critics_take: A loose adaptation of the 81 chapters of the Tao Te Ching, rewritten as advice for group facilitators and leaders. It has remained popular in management and counseling circles, though scholars point out that it is an interpretation, not a translation.

title: 59 Illustrated National Parks
author: Joel Anderson, Nathan Anderson
critics_take: A collection of retro WPA-style travel posters for each U.S. national park, produced by Anderson Design Group, with short notes on each park. Readers value it as a gift and coffee-table book; it is a design book rather than a guide.

title: ತೊತ್ತ (Totta)
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: Unaccustomed Earth
author: Jhumpa Lahiri
critics_take: Eight stories about Bengali-American families, including a linked trilogy about Hema and Kaushik, exploring the distance between immigrant parents and their American children. It debuted at number one on the New York Times bestseller list and won the Frank O'Connor International Short Story Award; critics praised its restraint and emotional precision.

title: Wide Sargasso Sea
author: Jean Rhys
critics_take: A prequel to Jane Eyre telling the story of Antoinette Cosway, the Creole heiress who becomes Rochester's "madwoman in the attic", from her childhood in post-emancipation Jamaica to her marriage. It is widely seen as a landmark of postcolonial and feminist fiction, and critics praise its compression and its reframing of Brontë's novel.

title: The Art of Mandala
critics_take: Not yet identified — title read from a shelf photo.

title: The Essential James Joyce
author: James Joyce; Harry Levin (ed.)
critics_take: A one-volume selection edited by the Harvard critic Harry Levin, including A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Dubliners, Exiles and selections from Ulysses and Finnegans Wake, along with poems. It has long served as a standard introduction to Joyce; critics value Levin's introductions while noting that excerpts can't convey the larger novels.

title: The Sea-Wolf
author: Jack London
critics_take: A literary critic, Humphrey van Weyden, is rescued after a shipwreck by the sealing schooner Ghost and forced to serve under its brutal, Nietzschean captain, Wolf Larsen. It was a bestseller and is admired for the figure of Larsen and its sea scenes, though critics find the romance in the second half weaker.

title: Notes to Myself: My Struggle to Become a Person
author: Hugh Prather
critics_take: A book of short journal entries and aphorisms recording the author's efforts to understand himself, his relationships and his feelings. It sold millions of copies and became a cult classic of the human-potential era; later readers often find it of its time.

title: The Start-Up J Curve: The Six Steps to Entrepreneurial Success
author: Howard Love
critics_take: A serial entrepreneur and investor describes a six-stage model of startup growth (Create, Release, Morph, Model, Scale, Harvest) shaped like a J curve. Readers found it a useful practical framework for founders; it received limited mainstream critical attention.

title: Don't Say Yes When You Want to Say No
author: Herbert Fensterheim and Jean Baer
critics_take: A guide to assertiveness training from the 1970s, based on behavior therapy, with exercises for expressing needs and refusing requests at work, at home and in relationships. It was a bestseller that helped popularize assertiveness training; it is now seen as a period classic of the genre.

title: Great Short Works of Henry James
author: Henry James
critics_take: A Harper Perennial collection of James's shorter fiction, including Daisy Miller, The Turn of the Screw, The Aspern Papers and The Beast in the Jungle. These novellas and tales are widely regarded as among his finest and most accessible work, showing his psychological subtlety in compact form.

title: The Education of Henry Adams
author: Henry Adams
critics_take: Adams's autobiography, written in the third person, follows the descendant of two presidents through 19th-century America and Europe and argues that his education left him unready for a world transformed by technology (the famous "Dynamo and the Virgin" chapter). It won the 1919 Pulitzer Prize and was named the top nonfiction book of the century by the Modern Library; critics admire its ironic voice while noting its self-pity and elisions, including his wife's suicide.

title: Golden Bats and Pink Pigeons
author: Gerald Durrell
critics_take: Durrell's account of an expedition to Mauritius and Rodrigues to collect endangered species such as the pink pigeon and the Rodrigues fruit bat for captive breeding at Jersey Zoo. Readers enjoy it for his usual comic animal writing; it is also valued as an early record of conservation breeding work.

title: Deer Man: Seven Years of Living in the Wild
author: Geoffroy Delorme
critics_take: Delorme's memoir of living for years among roe deer in a Normandy forest, sleeping outdoors and gradually being accepted by the herd. It was an international bestseller praised as an intimate nature memoir, though some reviewers raised questions about its plausibility and its rather mystical tone.

title: Deep Thinking: Where Machine Intelligence Ends and Human Creativity Begins
author: Garry Kasparov
critics_take: Kasparov revisits his 1996 and 1997 matches against IBM's Deep Blue and uses them to argue for optimism about human-machine collaboration in the age of AI. Reviewers found its chess history engaging and its account of the loss more generous than his earlier accusations, though its broader AI arguments were seen as less original.

title: Innocent Eréndira and Other Stories
author: Gabriel García Márquez
critics_take: An English collection pairing the novella The Incredible and Sad Tale of Innocent Eréndira and Her Heartless Grandmother, about a girl forced into prostitution by her grandmother, with early stories. Critics consider the title novella a vivid example of his magical realism; the early stories are generally regarded as apprentice work.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
critics_take: An impoverished former student, Raskolnikov, murders a pawnbroker to test his theory that extraordinary men may step outside morality, and then unravels under guilt and the pursuit of the investigator Porfiry. It is regarded as one of the greatest novels ever written, central to the psychological novel and to existentialist thought, though some critics find the redemptive epilogue unconvincing.

title: What They Really Teach You at the Harvard Business School
author: Francis J. Kelly and Heather Mayfield Kelly
critics_take: Written partly in response to McCormack's bestseller, the book summarizes the core MBA curriculum (marketing, finance, operations, organizational behavior and the case method) for general readers. It was received as a useful overview of HBS teaching, now dated.
